content.overview: Airflow quality is a distribution problem, not a fan-speed number. Strong local jets can coexist with stagnant interior canopy zones, so airflow should be interpreted through crop-zone measurements and spatial patterns.

vocabulary.definition: Movement that reduces unwanted spatial gradients in temperature, humidity and gas concentration.
A focused high-velocity air path that can over-dry nearby tissue without improving whole-canopy mixing.
A crop area with weak air exchange relative to surrounding positions.

sections.title: High velocity is not the same as good distribution
sections.body: Leaves nearest a fan can experience strong drying while dense interior canopy remains humid. Evaluate multiple positions rather than treating fan speed as the control variable.

sections.title: Map gradients against crop response
sections.body: Compare temperature/RH and crop findings across supply paths, returns, walls, aisles and canopy interiors. Spatial agreement can reveal whether airflow distribution is contributing to the problem.

sections.title: Do not redesign from one snapshot
sections.body: Repeat measurements across operating transitions and crop states. Persistent patterns are more informative than one short reading.

workedExamples: Fast drying next to a circulation fan plus high humidity inside the canopy suggests an uneven distribution problem rather than insufficient fan speed everywhere.
commonMistakes: Adding fan speed to already stressed leaves.
Using one wall sensor as proof of canopy mixing.
content.practicalApplication: Create an airflow/microclimate map using crop-zone temperature/RH points, visible plant response and fan/supply/return locations.
content.summary: Airflow should be judged by how evenly the crop environment responds, not by equipment speed alone.
